name: Crimson
lede: Crimson is a deep red with a lean toward purple, named after the kermes insect whose dye made it one of the costliest cloth colors of medieval Europe, and later the color of cochineal, of cardinals and of the painter's transparent red glaze.

sections.title: A word from a worm
sections.body:
Crimson is a deep red that leans toward purple, and for most of its history the word named a dye before it named a hue [24][32]. That dye came from kermes, a tiny scale insect, and the name travels with it. Greenfield traces crimson to the Arabic *kirmiz*, the word for the insect reds, while Ball and the Pigment Compendium carry the chain back to a Sanskrit word meaning made by a worm [7][1][17]. The two accounts fit together: the Sanskrit root passed through Persian and Arabic into the languages of Europe [17].

The same root gave French *cramoisi*, German *Karmesin* and the English word carmine [17][22]. Medieval English spelled it a dozen ways, among them *cremosin*, *cremesin* and *cramoisy* [32][17]. Our records date the word's arrival in English to around 1400, by way of Medieval Latin [36]. Finlay notes that Persian speakers still use the word kermes when they want to say red [22].

The ancients did not know the dye came from an animal. Theophrastus called the dried insects *kokkos*, a berry, and Pliny used *coccus* and *granum*, grain [1]. Hebrew was closer to the truth with *tola'at shani*, worm scarlet [1]. Chaucer's cloth dyed in grain was cloth dyed crimson, and because that red did not wash out, the phrase came to mean deeply and permanently dyed, which is where English gets the word ingrained [1][26].

sections.title: Kermes, lac and cochineal
sections.body:
The kermes insect lives on the kermes oak of southern and eastern Europe [26]. Dyers scraped the wingless females from the branches, crushed them and boiled them to free the red [26]. St Clair puts the yield at up to 80 insects for a single gram of dye, which made the color bright, fast and very dear [24]. Coles passes on a claim that Roman Spain paid half its taxes to Rome in kermes, a striking figure that no other book here repeats [26].

Painters needed the dye in solid form, so it was fixed onto a colorless powder to make a lake pigment. The word lake once meant red alone, and Paterson ties it to lac, an Indian insect resin whose color he gives as crimson [9][32]. Lac lakes were common in fifteenth-century Florence, and painters seem to have preferred these purplish crimson lakes to paler violet extracts [2]. Brazilwood gave cheaper crimsons too, but they faded to a dull pinkish brown, which earned the dye a reputation for deceit [7].

The great change came from Mexico [27]. Cochineal, a scale insect that feeds on prickly pear cactus, carries carminic acid, and Greenfield reckons it about ten times as strong as kermes [9][24]. The books agree that a pound of dye took tens of thousands of dried insects [28][24][19]. Their counts differ widely: Garfield gives 17,000 for an ounce, St Clair about 70,000 for a pound, and Pastoureau about 150,000 for a kilogram [28][24][19].

According to the Pigment Compendium, crimson at first named the color of every scale-insect dye [16]. Cochineal was so much stronger that the others were eventually dropped, and by the nineteenth century crimson lake simply meant a cochineal lake [16]. An 1869 handbook describes it as carmine stretched with more white base, weaker in color and less stable [16].

sections.title: The color of princes
sections.body:
Crimson was a sign of rank long before it was a paint. Isaiah, in the eighth century BC, chose scarlet and crimson as the colors of blood and sin [1]. In medieval cloth markets the word scarlet first named a fine woollen cloth, whatever its color; since such cloth was usually dyed with kermes, scarlet came to mean the dye and then the hue by the fourteenth century [5][7]. In the generalization Greenfield allows, crimson was the purplish of the two reds and scarlet the brighter [7].

Kings dressed in it from head to toe. Richard II of England was crowned in a crimson gown, with crimson hose and shoes to match, and in France the royal chancellor wore crimson while royal magistrates wore scarlet [7]. In Venice, men in the best crimson silk were said to dress like princes [7]. Pastoureau records that in 1245 Pope Innocent IV gave cardinals a red hat as their insignia, and Gurney notes that cardinals' robes were later dyed with cochineal [20][30].

Florence put a price on the hierarchy. A fifteenth-century Florentine dyers' manual called the kermes red the first and highest of all colors, and the city's sumptuary rules of 1464 named it [5][14]. Blue cloth, by the same manual, cost about half as much to dye [14]. Alessandra Strozzi, writing to her son, was delighted that her daughter's engagement present was a waistcoat of crimson velvet, the most beautiful cloth in Florence in her opinion [14].

Christian writers made the color sacred as well as costly. In the third century Cyprian of Carthage wrote that the Church, once clothed in white, was now dressed in crimson by the blood of its martyrs [18]. Pastoureau also shows translators adding the color where the original had none: a Greek phrase for royal clothing became a crimson cloak in later French [18].

sections.title: Cochineal and the Spanish crimson
sections.body:
When Cortés entered the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan in 1519, he found its markets full of yarn dyed a brilliant crimson [27]. He directed the final siege of the city from a tent with a crimson canopy [8]. A year later a Spanish merchant in the Americas boasted to his partner in Seville of selling crimson satin at three pesos a yard [8].

Books disagree on when the insect itself reached Europe in quantity [19][8]. Pastoureau dates the first exports to around 1525 to 1530, while Greenfield finds regular shipments to Seville only by the early 1540s, and the Pigment Compendium also gives the 1540s [19][8][16]. In February 1543, six master dyers in Venice tested three cochineal samples on silk against the best traditional crimson and swore under oath that they matched the finest kermes [9]. Genoa banned the new Indian kermes on silk the same year, then allowed it in 1550 [9].

The dye kept its royal meaning on both sides of the ocean. When Túpac Amaru, the last Inca ruler, was executed in 1572, an eyewitness recorded that he wore a mantle and doublet of crimson velvet [24]. In Europe, black became the fashion at court, but sitters were painted against crimson and scarlet draperies as a code for wealth; Van Dyck kept such draperies in his studio [9].

Chemistry could push the color either way. Around 1606 the Dutch inventor Cornelis Drebbel found that tin turned cochineal's dark crimson-purple into a blazing scarlet [10]. The popular tale says he found it by accident; Greenfield doubts that story and finds little evidence for the rival account either [10]. Isaac Newton, whose notebooks are full of red dye recipes, furnished his house with crimson curtains, cushions, bed hangings and a crimson settee [11].

sections.title: Crimson in painting
sections.body:
In paint, crimson is a glaze. Crimson lake is transparent, so painters laid it thinly over something brighter and let light pass through it. In 1434 the Flemish painter Saladijn de Stoevere was told that his Virgin's gold robe was to be glazed with crimson lake [3]. Sassetta, in his panels of the life of Saint Francis, laid silver leaf under a transparent kermes glaze to make the saint's red robe shine [14].

Many of the great reds of the next two centuries are crimsons. Jan van Eyck's *Virgin with Chancellor Rolin*, of about 1437, dresses the Madonna in crimson rather than the older ultramarine, a purplish red that recalls the purple of antiquity [5]. Bronzino's *[[art:commons-Q1990128|Portrait of Lucrezia Panciatichi]]* shows a red dress with sleeves of crimson and scarlet silk [7]. Delilah's dress in Rubens's *Samson and Delilah*, of about 1609, is almost pure crimson lake, brightened with a little [[vermilion]] and lead white [4].

The method survived into modern art. When Mondrian wanted a categorically pure red in the 1920s, he found, like painters before him, that he could get it only by glazing a bluish transparent crimson over an opaque orange-red such as vermilion [15]. A crimson lake also went into [[payne-s-grey]], which William Payne mixed from [[prussian-blue]], yellow ochre and crimson lake [25].

Crimson's weakness is light. Turner's carmine sunsets have faded, and where the pigment survives it reads as a deep crimson [22]. Alizarin crimson, made synthetically from 1868, was the next answer, but Gurney notes that it rates only III or IV for lightfastness and will eventually fade too; quinacridone, pyrrole and perylene reds now take its place [30]. Rothko's Harvard murals show the danger at its worst: he mixed his crimsons with a fugitive Lithol Red, and those dark pinks and crimsons have turned light blue [6].

sections.title: Out of fashion, into chemistry
sections.body:
Fashion turned away from crimson more than once. Pastoureau describes the seventeenth century's taste for darker reds, crimson and wine shades, and the Enlightenment's retreat from crimsons toward pastels [19][21]. During the French Revolution crimson velvet coats became a dangerous thing to wear, and by 1808 Mexican cochineal output had fallen to a third of its level in the 1770s [12]. In the nineteenth century, London fashion manuals told ladies of taste never to wear crimson or scarlet [12].

The aniline dyes ended cochineal's long reign. In 1858 August Hofmann reported a crimson coloring matter made from aniline, and in 1858 to 1859 the French chemist Emmanuel Verguin made a rich crimson dye he called fuchsine [29]. Renamed for the battles of 1859, it became [[magenta]] and [[solferino]] [29][13]. Cochineal fell from 15 francs a kilogram in 1858 to 8 a few years later [29].

sections.title: Where to see crimson
sections.body:
Crimson is easiest to see where light passes through something red. Gurney points out that a person's ears turn crimson when they are lit from behind, because light scatters inside the skin [31]. Rubies show both sides of the family at once: looked at along one axis a stone is crimson-pink, and across it, quite orange [23].

The same rule explains the painters' glazes. A thin transparent crimson over a bright ground glows; the same pigment laid thick looks dark and nearly purple [15][3]. Compare it with [[scarlet]], which leans toward orange, and [[carmine]], the deeper cochineal red; [[maroon]] and [[burgundy]] are crimson's browner, darker relatives.

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The swatch on this page is the web's `crimson`, one of the 140 X11 colors [32]. It is a vivid, slightly bluish red, brighter than most historical crimson cloth [36]. Other sources disagree about how dark crimson should be: the crowd-sourced xkcd survey placed it near a deep wine red, far darker than the web value [36].

Old swatches drift too. Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*, in Syme's 1821 edition, gave precious garnet as its example of Crimson Red, but the surviving chart has faded to something close to [[dusty-rose]] [36][34]. Treat any single chip as one reading of a family that runs from kermes red to cochineal purple.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a screen color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 11 works [35]. The web's crimson is far more saturated than most old paint photographs as, so the near-absence is itself a finding: a crimson glaze under old varnish reads darker and duller than the screen value [35].

Where it does appear it tends to be fresh and modern. Eight of the 11 works are Chinese, 27 times the archive's rate, mostly the pages of an illustrated book of flowers and butterflies from about 1800 [35]. The canvas where it covers most is José Benlliure y Gil's *[[art:commons-Q59859476|A Cardinal]]* of 1880, at 24 per cent of the image [35]. The earliest dated match is a 1633 landscape by Gillis Peeters, a reminder that small red accents can match without any crimson pigment [35].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [35]. The word has its own curve: in Google Books *crimson* peaks around 1862, and by 2000 it is printed about a fifth as often [37].

questions.q: Why did painters from Sassetta to Mondrian lay crimson thinly over something brighter?
choices: Crimson lake is transparent, so it glows as a glaze over a light or orange-red ground
Crimson was too expensive to use thickly anywhere
Crimson dries only in thin layers
Crimson turns blue when used thickly

openers: Crimson is named after an insect: kermes, which medieval writers mistook for a berry and called grain.
To be dyed in grain once meant dyed crimson; it is why we still call habits ingrained.
Look at someone's ears with the sun behind them: the glow is crimson, light passing through red.
